description: I'm a Systems Engineer with a Master's in AI and over four years of experience at Nokia as a Core Software Systems Engineer. I'm passionate about using AI to solve real-world problems. Our goal is to build FireScope AI, a platform combining satellite data, machine learning, and geospatial visualization to analyze historical fire activity and forecast regional wildfire risk. We're looking for people interested in Earth science, AI, data analysis, and web development.
summary:
FireScope AI: From Satellite Hotspots to Actionable Wildfire Intelligence

FireScope AI is an open-source geospatial intelligence project designed to harmonize NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations and establish the foundation for future early wildfire detection capabilities.

The project addresses the challenge of integrating observations from different satellite instruments, whose detection characteristics, spatial resolutions, and temporal coverage are not directly equivalent.

I developed a reproducible Python-based processing and analytical pipeline that ingests, standardizes, georeferences, and analyzes more than  14.29 million satellite detections  across the United States.

The current implementation includes historical activity analysis, seasonal climatology, retrospective anomaly detection, and experimentally evaluated machine learning models using independent temporal validation.

The development roadmap extends this foundation into a FastAPI backend, an interactive geospatial dashboard, integration testing, and deployment. Future research will focus on scientifically validated early-warning capabilities.

FireScope AI aims to make complex satellite observations more accessible, transparent, and useful for wildfire research, environmental monitoring, and decision support.
details:
FireScope AI — Harmonizing Satellite Observations for Wildfire Intelligence

The Problem

NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites provide valuable observations of active fires worldwide. However, their measurements cannot be compared directly because the instruments differ in spatial resolution, detection sensitivity, observation frequency, and satellite coverage.

Simply merging hotspot records can produce misleading conclusions. Furthermore, satellite detections do not necessarily represent individual wildfires, burned area, fire severity, or wildfire probability.

FireScope AI addresses this challenge by creating a transparent, reproducible platform for understanding historical satellite-detected burning activity.

The Solution

FireScope AI is an open-source geospatial intelligence application that transforms NASA satellite observations into accessible historical fire analytics.

The implemented MVP combines three components:

  1. A reproducible scientific data-processing pipeline.
  2. A read-only FastAPI analytical backend.
  3. An interactive React dashboard.

The application enables users to explore historical fire activity across the United States, examine seasonal patterns, identify retrospective anomalies, and understand experimental machine learning results.

FireScope AI emphasizes scientific transparency by distinguishing observed satellite detections from statistical estimates and explaining the limitations of each method.

The long-term objective is to support research toward earlier identification of potentially significant wildfire activity. Operational early-warning capabilities remain a future research goal.

What I Have Developed

Phase 1 — NASA Satellite Data Ingestion: Completed

I implemented a reproducible ingestion workflow using NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire datasets covering the United States.

The pipeline processed 14,290,135 satellite detections from three sensor groups:

  • MODIS Terra/Aqua.
  • VIIRS SNPP.
  • VIIRS NOAA-20.

The workflow preserves sensor provenance and converts the observations into structured analytical datasets.

Phase 2 — Harmonization and Historical Analysis: Completed

I developed processing workflows for data auditing, normalization, geographic attribution, temporal aggregation, exploratory cross-sensor harmonization, and historical climatology.

The system supports geographic analysis by U.S. state and H3 spatial indexing.

Historical datasets preserve sensor identity and support comparisons across geographic regions, time periods, and satellite instruments.

Exploratory harmonization does not establish that MODIS and VIIRS observations are physically interchangeable.

Phase 3 — Experimental Machine Learning and Scientific Validation: Completed

I implemented retrospective anomaly analysis, historical feature engineering, sensor-specific Ridge regression models, and independent chronological validation.

The evaluation separates three periods:

Stage

Period

Training

Through 2021

Model selection

2022–2023

Independent testing

2024–2025

The evaluation produced 3,341 independent test predictions.

Independent-test results were:

Satellite sensor

Improvement over seasonal baseline

MODIS

+2.16%

VIIRS SNPP

+1.71%

VIIRS NOAA-20

−3.78%

The models modestly outperformed the seasonal benchmark for MODIS and VIIRS SNPP but performed worse for VIIRS NOAA-20.

These comparisons use mean absolute error on log-transformed satellite detection counts.

The negative NOAA-20 result is explicitly documented.

These results are retrospective and experimental, not validated operational wildfire forecasts.

Phase 3.5 — Scientific Readiness: Implemented

I implemented scientific readiness checks and a release policy that limits the MVP to historical analytics.

The current release decision is:

historical_analytics_only

The application permits historical satellite observations, seasonal climatology, retrospective anomalies, and experimental retrospective model evaluation.

It does not present model estimates as validated future wildfire predictions or early-warning alerts.

Phase 4 — Analytical Backend API: Implemented

I developed a read-only analytical backend using Python, FastAPI, DuckDB, and Parquet.

The application exposes five API endpoint families:

  • /api/v1/regions
  • /api/v1/calendar
  • /api/v1/forecasts
  • /api/v1/anomalies
  • /api/v1/preparedness

These endpoints provide structured historical analytics and experimental model evaluation data.

The backend is implemented for the MVP, but an independently audited production deployment is not claimed.

Phase 5 — Interactive Dashboard: Implemented

I developed an interactive frontend using React, TypeScript, and Vite.

The dashboard contains four principal views:

1. Overview

Displays historical satellite detection metrics, geographic context, and temporal activity patterns.

2. Fire Calendar

Shows monthly satellite-detected fire activity and historical seasonal patterns.

3. Historical Anomalies

Compares observed monthly detection counts against historical averages for comparable calendar months.

The displayed deviations describe historical differences, not wildfire probabilities.

4. Experimental Model

Compares observed satellite detection counts with retrospective model estimates and displays evaluation errors.

The interface identifies the model as experimental rather than operational.

The application includes responsive navigation, geographic and temporal filters, and shared data caching.

Phase 6 — Integration and Engineering Validation: Partially Completed

I integrated the analytical backend with the React frontend and completed engineering validation checks.

Reported results include:

  • Frontend ESLint checks passed.
  • TypeScript and Vite production build passed.
  • 133 backend automated tests passed.

Further work includes independently verified deployment, automated data refresh, production monitoring, and broader reproducibility testing.

Phase 7 — MVP Demonstration and Documentation: Completed

I prepared the interactive MVP, technical documentation, scientific limitations, and a demonstration video.

The project repository contains the implementation, analytical methodology, model evaluation results, and supporting presentation materials.

The demonstration video is approximately 15 seconds long, within the NASA Space Apps Challenge's 30-second limit.

Technology Stack

Scientific processing and backend: Python, FastAPI, DuckDB, Apache Parquet, scikit-learn, and H3.

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, and React Query.

Development and testing: Git, GitHub, pytest, ESLint, and TypeScript.

The project follows Clean Architecture principles to separate scientific processing, application logic, infrastructure, and presentation.

Innovation

FireScope AI combines scientific reproducibility with accessible visualization of NASA satellite observations.

Its main contributions are:

  1. Multi-instrument analysis: preserving MODIS and VIIRS sensor identity.
  2. Scalable processing: analyzing more than 14.29 million satellite detections.
  3. Geographic and seasonal analysis: connecting observations with regional historical patterns.
  4. Retrospective anomaly detection: identifying unusual historical activity.
  5. Transparent machine learning: independently evaluating models and reporting negative results.
  6. Interactive visualization: making analytical outputs accessible through a web dashboard.
  7. Responsible communication: distinguishing measured observations from experimental estimates.

Intended Impact

FireScope AI aims to make NASA satellite fire observations easier to explore, compare, and interpret.

Potential beneficiaries include wildfire researchers, environmental analysts, educators, land-management organizations, and teams studying historical burning patterns.

The platform provides an accessible foundation for investigating seasonal and geographic differences in satellite-detected fire activity.

With additional research and validation, this foundation could support future wildfire monitoring and early-detection studies.

Scientific Limitations

FireScope AI is a historical analytics and experimental research application, not an operational wildfire warning system.

The current MVP does not:

  • Estimate calibrated wildfire occurrence probabilities.
  • Identify unique wildfire events.
  • Measure burned area or wildfire severity.
  • Fully correct satellite observation coverage differences.
  • Provide validated future-date wildfire forecasts.
  • Issue operational early-warning alerts.

Machine learning results are retrospective, sensor-specific, and experimental.

The independent evaluation showed modest improvements for two sensors and worse performance for VIIRS NOAA-20.

These limitations are documented to support responsible interpretation.

Future Research

Future development may explore:

  • More timely satellite-data ingestion.
  • Weather and vegetation variables.
  • Improved treatment of satellite coverage.
  • Uncertainty quantification.
  • Multi-horizon model evaluation.
  • Independently validated wildfire-risk models.
  • Production deployment and monitoring.

Early wildfire detection remains a research objective rather than a validated feature of the current MVP.

Project Repository and Demonstration

Project source code and documentation:

https://github.com/Ljara20/FireScopeAI

Demonstration video and supporting materials:

The video can be accessed through its GitHub file page or downloaded for playback.
